idiom_name: ReadWriteProperty delegate whose getValue caches and setValue invalidates
implementation_notes: Delegated properties are the local idiom: `val x: T by DirtyVar { compute() }` routes reads to the delegate's getValue (recompute when the slot is empty) and writes to setValue (empty the slot), so invalidation is structural instead of a duty at every call site. The delegate is a dozen lines against ReadWriteProperty, or a class with operator getValue/setValue; Kotlin's stdlib delegates cover the neighbouring cases but not this one - by lazy caches exactly once and can never be reset, while Delegates.observable gives a change hook without caching. For shared state use a @Volatile field with a double-checked accessor (see the other variant) or an atomic reference, because a delegated property has no thread-safety of its own.
pitfalls: A nullable cache conflates 'not computed' with 'computed null'; constrain T : Any or keep a separate Boolean - a legitimate null recomputes forever otherwise.
Each property instantiation allocates its delegate (and a delegate in the companion object would share one slot across all instances); remember the per-instance cost.
The delegate is not thread-safe: @Volatile on a delegate's field does not exist, so concurrent access needs explicit synchronization or the volatile-field variant.
Framework code that writes the property during construction or deserialization (DI, serializers) clears the cache after every assignment - invalidate only on real mutations.

variants.name: @Volatile field with double-checked recompute
variants.implementation_notes: For state reachable from several threads the canonical form is a private @Volatile field tested outside the lock and rebuilt inside synchronized, with the cache published before the flag/reference is updated. Kotlin deliberately annotates instead of adding a volatile keyword, and the documentation warns that volatile only guarantees linearizable reads and writes of that variable - it does not make larger actions atomic, so the recomputation itself still needs a lock (synchronized, Mutex or an atomic). This replaces the delegate for shared objects: the delegate is cleaner for single-threaded invariants, the volatile field for published ones.
pitfalls: @Volatile is linearizable per field but does not make a read-modify-write sequence atomic: `cache ?: rebuild()` outside the lock can rebuild twice (idempotent rebuilds only).
Without the lock's happens-before edge a partially constructed cache can be observed; keep the cached value immutable or build it inside the critical section.
synchronized on an instance exposes the monitor to external code; lock on a private object as above, or use kotlinx.atomicfu / AtomicReference.
On Kotlin/Native and Kotlin/JS the JVM @Volatile semantics do not exist - the annotation is JVM-only, so shared-state code must be reworked rather than copied.
